title: Mike Babcock downplays Leafs legacy talk ahead of return: ‘The Beatles broke up, remember?’
content:
TORONTO – Mike Babcock darted off the Scotiabank Arena ice after practice and turned right into a hallway toward the visitors dressing room instead of left, as he did hundreds of times before.

The Edmonton Oilers coach returned to Toronto as an NHL head coach for the first time since being fired as Toronto Maple Leafs coach in 2019. Babcock’s Oilers play the Leafs on Saturday night.

But on Friday, Babcock had little time to consider his legacy as one of the most notable coaches in recent Leafs history.

“I don’t spend a whole lot of time thinking about that,” Babcock said bluntly.

Still wearing one of his orange-and-blue gloves and leaning on his stick, Babcock addressed reporters the way he runs his practices: short and fast.

Babcock said he looked back on his time as Leafs coach fondly.

“I loved it,” Babcock said. “I worked with real good people. I enjoyed the heck out of my first three years here. We worked with good hockey men and it was enjoyable. I didn’t enjoy the last year-and-a-half as much. But that’s the business.”

Babcock was hired by former Leafs GM Lou Lamoriello in 2015. Before Babcock’s firing in 2019, Kyle Dubas took over as Leafs GM in 2018.

“We set a franchise record for points. We didn’t have enough success in the playoffs, but that’s often what happens with young teams,” Babcock said of his Leafs tenure. “In the end, (the Leafs) gave me a five-year holiday, which I really enjoyed.”

After taking three questions about being Leafs coach, Babcock sounded intent on moving on to his current Oilers team.

“This is five years ago, right? The Beatles broke up, remember?” Babcock said.

Babcock’s return brings the differing directions of his current and former teams into focus.

The Oilers currently sit second in the NHL standings in points percentage. Connor McDavid is in the middle of a 20-game point streak, with a league-leading 49 points over that span.

The Leafs meanwhile find themselves in the kind of skid Babcock went through just before his firing. They have lost five straight and seven of their last eight games and sit in second-last in the Atlantic Division. Babcock’s former Leafs assistant and current Leafs head coach, Jim Hiller, is now the one trying to right the ship.

“This is what I know about Jim Hiller: he’s a real good man, he’s a good person, he’s going to work hard and do his best every day and try to help the guys win. So that’s what I know,” Babcock said. “The NHL some days isn’t kind to you, but you’ve got to be kind to yourself, and you’ve got to enjoy what you’re doing. Shut off your apps or whatever the heck you got on your phone and get on with your life. The people (whose) knees hit your kitchen table matter; the rest of them don’t matter.”

Babcock’s return was a reminder of the way he once ran his Leafs teams.

The Oilers’ Friday practice was scheduled to begin at noon. But Babcock started things early, and by 11:58 a.m., he had already halted a drill to bark instructions at his team. His voice echoed above others through Scotiabank Arena.

Babcock played the hits through an uptempo practice.

“Let’s go!” he chanted repeatedly.

“You’ve gotta rub the guy,” he shouted at his defencemen.

Drills were quick. From one side of the ice to the other, from one group to the next, Babcock did not stop moving. Every touch of the puck was under his watch.

“There’s a bunch of them there that are just great pros that want to have success,” Babcock said of his Oilers players. “And so to be around them each day is fun. I’m trying to help them get better, and they’re trying to help me get better.”

Before being hired by the Leafs, Babcock coached the Anaheim Ducks and Detroit Red Wings. He won a Stanley Cup with the Red Wings in 2008. He was then brought on to overhaul a rebuilding Leafs team in 2015. His eight-year, reported $50-million contract made him the highest-paid coach in NHL history.

The Leafs made the playoffs in Babcock’s final three full seasons in Toronto, losing in the first round each time. Even after a dismal first season that led to the Leafs winning the draft lottery and landing Auston Matthews, Babcock still finished with a 173-133-45 record in Toronto.

Babcock was fired by the Leafs on Nov. 20, 2019, after a six-game losing streak. After his firing, he drew criticism for his handling of then-young Leaf Mitch Marner. Babcock asked Marner, then a rookie, to rank his teammates’ work ethic. Babcock showed the list to Marner’s teammates. He later said he apologized to Marner.

After serving as a volunteer coach at the University of Saskatchewan, Babcock was hired by the Columbus Blue Jackets in 2023. He did not coach a single game, however, after a report surfaced that he ordered players to show him their cell phone photos. Babcock resigned before the team’s training camp began.

Babcock was hired by the Oilers in June. He is currently 12th among NHL coaches with 714 career regular-season wins.

“I’ve been fortunate to get to coach as long as I have and to enjoy it as much as I have, and I’m very thankful to the NHL for that,” Babcock said. “I think everything changes and what won last year can’t win the next year. You have to get better. You’ve got to embrace it. And so I think that’s where the fun is, though, is trying to get better. That’s what you want to do in life, and that’s what you want to do in hockey and anything you do.”
